summary.title: Famous laws of Software development
summary.one_liner: A tour of fourteen well-known software development laws and principles (Murphy's, Brooks's, Conway's, Linus's, Moore's and others), with each law's statement and the author's interpretation.
keywords: brook's law adding manpower late project
given enough eyeballs all bugs are shallow
wirth's law software slower than hardware
why adding developers makes project later
takeaways: Brooks's law: adding people to a late project tends to make it later; review efficiency, methodology and architecture first.
Conway's law: software mirrors the communication structure of the organization, so structure teams around the target architecture (e.g. bounded contexts).
Hofstadter's law: tasks always take longer than expected, even after accounting for this law, so pad estimates with a buffer.
Linus's law and Knuth's principle: wide code review finds bugs quickly, and premature optimization should wait until bottlenecks are identified.
Pareto (80-20), Peter, Wirth, and Moore's laws are summarized with the author's interpretations; the page is an informal collection rather than a rigorous source.
summary.summary: The article is an informal collection of famous software development laws, principles and sayings, presented as an index followed by a short section per law. For each one it gives the statement (often with its origin, such as Brooks, Conway, Postel, Linus Torvalds or Moore), then the author's interpretation and suggested defenses or practical implications. It is written in a casual, opinionated tone and includes some humorous asides. It does not go deeply into evidence or formal treatment of any law.
